screen.title: Color Words and Perception
screen.directions: Read an Academic Passage — upper module
text: Languages differ considerably in how they divide the color spectrum. Russian, for instance, obligatorily distinguishes between lighter blues (goluboy) and darker blues (siniy), whereas English speakers use a single basic term. This raises a question that has long intrigued linguists and psychologists: does the vocabulary a person habitually uses shape the way that person actually perceives the world?

Experimental evidence suggests a modest but measurable influence. In one study, Russian speakers distinguished between two shades of blue more rapidly when the shades straddled the boundary between goluboy and siniy than when both fell within a single category; English speakers showed no comparable advantage. Crucially, the effect vanished when participants simultaneously performed a verbal task that occupied their linguistic resources.

Researchers therefore caution against strong claims. Language does not appear to determine what people are capable of seeing; it seems instead to provide a convenient shortcut that accelerates certain judgments whenever linguistic processing is available.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
options: Russian speakers are able to see more colors than English speakers can.
Color terms can slightly speed up some visual decisions without limiting what people perceive.
Doing a verbal task improves people's ability to tell colors apart.
Linguists disagree about how many basic color terms each language has.

why.en: Main idea (paraphrase). A is too extreme; C contradicts the text.
why.tr: Ana fikir (parafraz). A aşırı uç; C metnin tersi.
why.es: Idea principal (paráfrasis). A es demasiado extremo; C contradice el texto.

questions.stem: The word "straddled" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
options: avoided
matched
crossed
darkened

why.en: Vocabulary in context: straddle the boundary = fall on both sides of the boundary, cross it.
why.tr: Bağlamda kelime: straddle the boundary = sınırın iki yanına düşmek, sınırı geçmek.
why.es: Vocabulario en contexto: straddle the boundary = quedar a ambos lados del límite, cruzarlo.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention the verbal task?
options: To describe a common method of teaching color names
To explain why English speakers performed poorly overall
To prove that Russian speakers have sharper eyesight
To show that the advantage depends on language being actively engaged

why.en: Author's purpose: the effect disappears when language resources are busy → the advantage depends on actively using language.
why.tr: Yazarın amacı: etki dil kaynakları meşgulken kayboluyor → avantaj dilin aktif kullanımına bağlı.
why.es: Propósito del autor: el efecto desaparece cuando los recursos lingüísticos están ocupados → la ventaja depende de usar activamente el lenguaje.

questions.stem: What would the researchers most likely say about the claim that speakers cannot see a color their language has no word for?
options: It goes further than the evidence supports.
It is fully confirmed by the Russian study's results.
It explains why the effect vanished.
It applies only to shades of blue.

why.en: Inference: "caution against strong claims" → it goes beyond the evidence.
why.tr: Çıkarım: "caution against strong claims" → kanıtın ötesine geçiyor.
why.es: Inferencia: "caution against strong claims" → va más allá de las pruebas.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, when did Russian speakers respond faster?
options: When both shades were dark blue
When the two shades fell on different sides of the category boundary
When they were also doing a verbal task
When English speakers had answered first

why.en: Detail: shades on both sides of the boundary = groups with different names. C contradicts the text.
why.tr: Detay : sınırın iki yanındaki tonlar = farklı adlandırılmış gruplar. C metnin tersi.
why.es: Detalle: tonos a ambos lados del límite = grupos con nombres distintos. C contradice el texto.
